steps.rendered_prompt:
You are writing a short explainer script from a research record.

Audience: General public with secondary-school science literacy
Target spoken duration: about 60 seconds.

Write the script from the research record below. Make it accurate and easy to follow.

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it, in exactly this shape:

{
  "case_id": "C08",
  "audience": "General public with secondary-school science literacy",
  "target_duration_s": 60,
  "beats": [
    {"beat": "short label", "narration": "what the narrator says",
     "on_screen": "what is shown", "claim_refs": []}
  ]
}

RESEARCH RECORD
---------------
Immune memory and the filing-cabinet analogy, with its stated breakdown point

Record
SYN-C08

Study design
Review with an explicitly bounded teaching analogy

Background
After an infection resolves, a subset of antigen-specific T cells persists as a memory population capable of a faster and larger response on re-exposure. How long that population remains detectable, and how the speed of the secondary response compares with the primary, are practical questions for vaccine scheduling and for how immunity is explained to the public. This review quantifies both in a single cohort using a defined viral epitope.

Abstract
Memory T cells persist after infection and enable a faster secondary response. In this review we quantify persistence: in a cohort of 302 adults, antigen-specific memory CD8+ T cells against a defined viral epitope were detectable in 88% of participants at 5 years and in 61% at 12 years. Secondary expansion on re-exposure was 4.2-fold faster than the primary response.

Methods
Detection was by MHC-multimer staining; persistence figures are cohort-level and vary by pathogen and by individual. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were stained with MHC class I multimers loaded with the defined epitope and analysed by flow cytometry. A participant was scored positive above a fixed frequency threshold. Secondary expansion was measured in a subset re-exposed under a controlled protocol.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis: detection frequencies are reported with exact binomial confidence intervals: 88% (95% CI 84 to 91) at 5 years and 61% (95% CI 55 to 67) at 12 years. The 4.2-fold secondary expansion figure is a geometric mean ratio across the re-exposed subset (n = 34, 95% CI 3.1 to 5.7). Participants contributing at both timepoints were analysed as paired observations. Assay performance was monitored with a fixed control sample across batches.

Results
  endpoint: Memory CD8+ T cells detectable at 5 years; value: 88% of participants
  endpoint: Memory CD8+ T cells detectable at 12 years; value: 61% of participants
  endpoint: Secondary expansion speed; value: 4.2-fold faster than primary

Teaching note
  analogy: Immune memory is sometimes introduced to students as a filing cabinet: the body keeps a folder on a pathogen it has met, so it can act faster next time.
  note: The comparison holds for speed of the secondary response. It does not hold for retrieval or permanence: memory populations are not indexed, are not queried on demand, and decline over time, as the 5-year and 12-year detection figures show. Detectable memory cells also do not guarantee protection from disease.

Discussion
Quantifying the persistence of antigen-specific memory populations is important both for vaccine schedule design and for public communication. Teaching analogies are valuable in the latter context provided their scope is respected.

Limitations
  Persistence figures are for one defined viral epitope and vary by pathogen and individual.

Conclusion
Memory CD8+ T cells persisted for years in most participants and the secondary response expanded 4.2-fold faster than the primary response.

Data availability
Flow cytometry standard files are deposited under accession SYN-C08.

beats.narration: Once you recover from an infection, your immune system doesn't forget it. Some of the T cells that fought the infection stick around as a memory population, ready for next time.
beats.on_screen: A virus particle fades out; a small group of T cells remains on screen, labelled 'memory T cells'.

beats.narration: A review of 302 adults measured how long that memory lasts for one specific viral target. Memory CD8 T cells were still detectable in 88 percent of people after five years, and in 61 percent after twelve.
beats.on_screen: Bar chart: 88% at 5 years, 61% at 12 years, with confidence intervals 84-91 and 55-67.

beats.narration: And when those people met the virus again, their immune response ramped up 4.2 times faster than the first time around.
beats.on_screen: Two response curves side by side: a slow primary rise, a steep secondary rise, tagged '4.2x faster'.

beats.narration: People often explain this like a filing cabinet: your body keeps a folder on every germ it has met, so it can pull it out fast.
beats.on_screen: Animated filing cabinet; a drawer opens and a labelled folder slides out.

beats.narration: That works for speed, but only for speed. Immune memory isn't indexed, nothing looks a file up on demand, and the folders fade with time, as those five and twelve year numbers show. Having memory cells also doesn't guarantee you won't get sick.
beats.on_screen: The filing cabinet dissolves; three struck-through captions appear: 'not indexed', 'not permanent', 'not a guarantee of protection'.

beats.narration: These figures come from one viral target and vary between pathogens and people, but knowing how memory fades is exactly what helps scientists decide when a booster is due.

final_narration:
Once you recover from an infection, your immune system doesn't forget it. Some of the T cells that fought the infection stick around as a memory population, ready for next time.
A review of 302 adults measured how long that memory lasts for one specific viral target. Memory CD8 T cells were still detectable in 88 percent of people after five years, and in 61 percent after twelve.
And when those people met the virus again, their immune response ramped up 4.2 times faster than the first time around.
People often explain this like a filing cabinet: your body keeps a folder on every germ it has met, so it can pull it out fast.
That works for speed, but only for speed. Immune memory isn't indexed, nothing looks a file up on demand, and the folders fade with time, as those five and twelve year numbers show. Having memory cells also doesn't guarantee you won't get sick.
These figures come from one viral target and vary between pathogens and people, but knowing how memory fades is exactly what helps scientists decide when a booster is due.
